_about: Text versions of the seed scenarios (same codes as email.json, so each scenario is one scam with a version per channel). Short enough for two text messages including the link. A reply to any of them counts as a practice opportunity unless it reads as worried or confused; reply_keywords are the answers each scenario invites. STOP, CANCEL, END, QUIT, HELP, START and REPORT are reserved.

scenarios.name: Parcel redelivery fee
scenarios.content: Parcel Notice: we couldn't deliver your package today. A $1.99 redelivery fee is due within 24 hrs or it returns to sender. Pay here: {link}

tells.note: Delivery companies don't text you asking for a fee. The small amount is there to get your card number.
The deadline hurries you past the moment you'd stop and check.
No company name and no tracking number. A real notice would have both.

next_steps: If I'm expecting something, I'll check the tracking number on the shop's own website.
I won't tap a link in a text to pay a fee.
I'll delete it.
scenarios.learning_objective: Fees by text for redelivery are a common way to collect card numbers.
scenarios.debrief: Fake delivery texts are among the most common scams going, because nearly everyone has a parcel on the way at some point. The fee is small on purpose. The goal is your card number.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A text asking you to pay a fee to redeliver a parcel
The text arriving during the day
question.affirm: That's right. A delivery company won't text you asking for a fee, so that alone is enough to delete it.
question.gently: Understandable, but the clearest sign is the fee. A delivery company won't text asking for money to try again.

scenarios.name: Sweepstakes win with a fee
scenarios.content: CONGRATS! Your number was selected to win $850,000 in our national sweepstakes. Reply CLAIM to receive your winnings. A small processing fee applies.

tells.note: You can't win a contest you never entered.
Real prizes don't cost money to collect. Paying to receive money is the scam.
Replying tells them your number is answered by a real person, and the next message asks for money.

next_steps: If I didn't enter, I didn't win, so I'll delete it.
I won't reply to a text from a number I don't know.
I won't pay anything to collect a prize.
scenarios.learning_objective: Paying a fee to collect a prize is the core of the prize scam.
scenarios.debrief: Prize texts have one request at their heart, which is to send a little money to receive a lot. Replying to them also marks your number as one a person answers, which brings more scam texts.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: Winning a contest you never entered, with a fee to collect
question.affirm: Yes. A contest you didn't enter and a fee to collect are the giveaway.
question.gently: Those stand out too, but the clearest sign is winning something you never entered, and being asked to pay to collect it.

scenarios.name: Virus warning with a phone number
scenarios.content: SECURITY ALERT: 5 viruses detected on your device. Your banking info may be exposed. Call a certified technician now or tap to fix: {link} Do NOT turn off your phone.

tells.note: Nobody can see viruses on your phone from the outside and text you about them.

tells.quote: Do NOT turn off your phone
tells.note: Turning it off is safe. This line is there to keep you anxious.
The 'technician' wants remote access to your device, then payment or your bank login.

next_steps: I'll delete the text and won't call or tap anything in it.
If I'm worried about my phone, I'll ask someone I know or visit the store where I bought it.
I won't let anyone I didn't contact first connect to my phone or computer.
scenarios.learning_objective: Unsolicited virus warnings that push you to contact a technician are tech support scams.
scenarios.debrief: Tech support scams start with a scare and end with someone connected to your device. Real security software doesn't text you a number to call.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A text claiming it can see viruses on your phone
Being told not to turn the phone off
question.affirm: That's it. Nobody can see what's on your phone from outside and text you about it.
question.gently: That line is meant to scare you, so it's a good one to notice. The first sign, though, is the claim itself: nobody can see your phone's contents from outside.

scenarios.name: Bank account locked
scenarios.content: Your Bank Alert: unusual sign-in detected. Your account has been locked. Verify your card number and PIN within 12 hrs to unlock: {link}

tells.note: Your real bank uses its own name and usually your name too.
No bank ever asks for your PIN, by text or any other way.
The deadline is there to rush you.

next_steps: I'll call the number on the back of my card and ask if anything's wrong.
I'll sign in the way I always do, never from a link in a text.
I'll never give my PIN to anyone.
scenarios.learning_objective: Your bank never asks for your PIN or card number by text.
scenarios.debrief: Account-locked texts work because they make your money feel in danger and offer a quick fix. If something really were wrong, calling the number on your card would tell you.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: It asks for your card number and PIN
question.affirm: Yes. A bank will never ask for your PIN, so that request alone gives it away.
question.gently: Real banks do mention unusual activity sometimes, which is why this is convincing. The giveaway is the request for your PIN.

scenarios.name: Power shut-off today
scenarios.content: FINAL NOTICE: your electric service will be disconnected TODAY at 4PM for a past-due balance of $186.42. To avoid shut-off, pay now by gift card or online: {link}

tells.note: Utilities send written notices over weeks before any shut-off. Same-day warnings by text are made up.
No utility takes gift cards. Anyone asking for one is running a scam.
Calling it final when you've had no earlier notice is a pressure trick.

next_steps: I'll call the number on my last paper bill and ask about my account.
I'll never pay a bill with a gift card.
I'll delete it.
scenarios.learning_objective: Same-day shut-off threats and gift card payments are utility scam signs.
scenarios.debrief: Utility scams lean on the worry of being without power. Real utilities give plenty of written notice and take ordinary payments.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: Being asked to pay by gift card
question.affirm: Right. No utility takes gift cards, so that request gives it away.
question.gently: The exact amount is meant to look official. The surest sign is the gift card: no utility takes them.

scenarios.name: Missed jury duty fine
scenarios.content: County Court Notice: you failed to appear for jury duty and a warrant may be issued. Pay the $495 fine today to cancel it: {link}

tells.note: Courts don't threaten arrest by text. A missed summons is handled by post.

tells.quote: Pay the $495 fine today to cancel it
tells.note: Courts don't take fines through text links, and paying never cancels a warrant.
It doesn't say which county or court. A real notice would.

next_steps: I'll look up the court's number myself and call to ask.
I won't pay a fine from a link in a text.
I'll tell someone in the family, since these scams count on embarrassment.
scenarios.learning_objective: Courts don't threaten arrest or collect fines by text.
scenarios.debrief: Jury duty scams work on worry and embarrassment. You can always call the clerk's office yourself, using a number you looked up.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: Being asked to pay a fine by text to cancel a warrant
The text arriving during the day
question.affirm: Yes. Courts don't take payment by text to make a warrant go away.
question.gently: Official-sounding words are part of the disguise. The clearest sign is the payment request.

scenarios.name: "It's me" from a new number
scenarios.content: Hi it's me, I lost my phone so this is my new number. I'm in a bit of trouble and need $600 today. Please don't tell Mom or Dad yet. Can you help? Reply YES and I'll explain

tells.note: Someone you know would use their name. 'It's me' lets you fill in who you think it is.
A new number stops you from calling the old one to check, which is exactly what to do.

tells.quote: Please don't tell Mom or Dad yet
tells.note: Keeping it secret keeps you from hearing that everyone is fine.

next_steps: I'll call them on the number I already have.
If I can't reach them, I'll call someone else in the family before I send anything.
I won't send money because of a text from a new number.
scenarios.learning_objective: "It's me" texts from a new number asking for urgent, secret money are family emergency scams.
scenarios.debrief: This is the text version of the grandparent scam, and it works because it lands on love and worry at once. Calling the number you already have settles it in a minute.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A new number, no name, and a request to keep it secret
question.affirm: Exactly. No name, a new number and a secret are how these keep you from checking.
question.gently: The amount can feel small, which is part of the trick. The clearest sign is the new number with no name and the request for secrecy.

scenarios.name: Disaster relief with a matching deadline
scenarios.content: Storm Relief Fund: families lost everything this week. Gifts are DOUBLED until midnight! Give $50 by gift card or wire, it reaches them fastest: {link}

tells.note: Real charities welcome gifts any time. A countdown stops you from looking the charity up first.
Established charities take cards and checks. Gift cards and wires can't be traced or refunded.
A name that sounds right but that you've never heard of is worth looking up before giving.

next_steps: I'll give to a charity I already know, on its own website.
I'll look up any charity I don't know before giving.
I won't give by gift card or wire.
scenarios.learning_objective: Fake charities use deadlines and untraceable payment methods.
scenarios.debrief: Fake charities appear after every disaster because generous people want to help fast. Giving through a charity you know, on its own website, gets your money where it should go.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: Asking for gift cards or a wire
question.affirm: Yes. Real charities don't ask for gift cards or wires.
question.gently: Mentioning real news is what makes these convincing. The clearest sign is the payment method.

scenarios.name: Medicare plan ending
scenarios.content: Medicare Benefits Office: your 2027 coverage has been flagged for changes. To avoid a gap in coverage, confirm your Medicare number within 48 hrs: {link}

tells.note: Open Enrollment runs for weeks. Nobody official gives you 48 hours.
Your Medicare number is used to bill for things you never got. Keep it for your doctors and pharmacy.
Medicare doesn't text you to ask for your number.

next_steps: I'll call the number on my Medicare card if I want to check my plan.
I won't type my Medicare number into a link from a text.
I'll review plans with someone I trust, like a local SHIP counselor.
scenarios.learning_objective: Medicare doesn't text asking for your Medicare number.
scenarios.debrief: This is harder because it arrives during real Open Enrollment, when you expect news about your plan. The short deadline and the request for your number give it away.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A request for your Medicare number with a 48-hour deadline
question.affirm: That's right. A short deadline plus a request for your Medicare number is the combination to watch for.
question.gently: It feels more believable because of the timing. The giveaway is the deadline and the request for your number.

scenarios.name: Tax refund waiting
scenarios.content: Tax Refund Dept: you are eligible for an additional refund of $1,284.00. Confirm your bank details and SSN to receive it by direct deposit: {link}

tells.quote: you are eligible for an additional refund
tells.note: The tax agency contacts people by post, not by text, and not to hand out surprise money.
Together these let someone take over accounts or file a return in your name.
No real agency signs a text this way.

next_steps: If I think I'm owed a refund, I'll check on the tax agency's website by typing the address myself.
I'll never send my Social Security number in reply to a text.
I'll delete it.
scenarios.learning_objective: The tax agency doesn't text about refunds or ask for your Social Security number.
scenarios.debrief: Good news can lower your guard, which is why refund texts work for some people. The request for your bank details and Social Security number is what to notice.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: Being asked for your bank details and Social Security number by text
question.affirm: Yes. Nobody official asks for those by text.
question.gently: The exact amount is there to seem believable. The clearest sign is the request for your Social Security number and bank details.

scenarios.name: Surprise renewal charge
scenarios.content: Billing Support: your Device Protection Plan renewed for $399.99. If you did not authorize this, reply REFUND within 24 hrs and an agent will call you.

tells.note: If you don't recognize the plan, that's because there isn't one. The surprise sends you straight to them.
The rush makes you act before checking your real statement.
The 'refund' call ends with someone on your computer or in your bank account.

next_steps: I'll check my card statement directly for the charge.
If I see a charge I don't recognize, I'll call the number on my card.
I won't reply to a receipt I don't recognize.
scenarios.learning_objective: Fake renewal notices push you to 'cancel' through a scammer.
scenarios.debrief: Fake receipts make you want to act to protect yourself, and that urge is the trap. Your real statement will tell you whether anything was charged.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A charge for a plan you never bought, with 24 hours to reply
question.affirm: Right. A charge you don't recognize with a short window is the setup.
question.gently: Prices ending in .99 are normal. The sign is a charge for something you never bought and a rush to respond.

scenarios.name: Friendly stranger, wrong number
scenarios.content: Hello, is this Linda? It's Daniel from the reunion. Sorry if I have the wrong number. You seem kind anyway. I'm working overseas and it's been a lonely year since my wife passed.

tells.quote: Sorry if I have the wrong number
tells.note: The 'wrong number' opener is a way to start chatting with a stranger without looking like a pitch.

tells.quote: it's been a lonely year since my wife passed
tells.note: Sharing a loss straight away builds sympathy fast. It's a common opening in romance scams.
Working abroad explains why they can never meet, and later why they need money.

next_steps: I won't keep chatting with someone who texted me by mistake.
I'll block numbers I don't know that try to start a conversation.
I'll never send money to someone I haven't met in person.
scenarios.learning_objective: "Wrong number" openers from lonely, overseas strangers are how romance scams begin.
scenarios.debrief: Romance scams start slowly and kindly, and money doesn't come up for weeks. The opening is the best place to spot them, and it follows a familiar pattern.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A stranger texting 'by mistake', sharing a loss and living overseas
question.affirm: Yes. That pattern is how these usually begin.
question.gently: Politeness is part of the charm. The pattern to notice is the wrong-number start, the shared loss and the job overseas.

scenarios.name: Voter registration problem
scenarios.content: Election Records Office: a problem with your voter registration may stop you voting this year. Confirm your DOB and last 4 of SSN to stay registered: {link}

tells.quote: a problem with your voter registration
tells.note: Election offices send problems by post, and you can check your registration on your state's official website.
Nobody needs your Social Security number by text to keep you registered.

tells.quote: may stop you voting this year
tells.note: The threat of losing your vote is there to make you act fast.

next_steps: I'll check my registration on my state's official election website.
I'll call my county election office if I'm unsure.
I won't give personal details through a link in a text.
scenarios.learning_objective: Election offices don't text asking for your Social Security number to keep you registered.
scenarios.debrief: Election scams pick up before a vote, when people care most about taking part. Checking your own registration takes a couple of minutes and is far safer than any link.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: It asks for part of your Social Security number by text
question.affirm: Right. No election office asks for that by text.
question.gently: The timing makes it feel real. The clearest sign is the request for part of your Social Security number.

scenarios.name: Benefits suspended
scenarios.content: Benefits Administration: your monthly benefits are SUSPENDED due to suspicious activity on your SSN. Call your case officer today to reinstate: {link} Case BA-2207-44

tells.note: A Social Security number can't be suspended, and benefits aren't stopped by text.
The 'case officer' is the scammer.
A reference number makes it look official. Anyone can make one up.

next_steps: I'll call the agency on a number I look up myself.
I'll check my benefits by signing in the usual way.
I won't call a 'case officer' named in a text.
scenarios.learning_objective: Benefits aren't suspended by text.
scenarios.debrief: Government impersonation takes a real worry, losing income you rely on, and dresses it up with official-sounding details. A call to the agency on a number you found yourself clears it up.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A text saying your benefits are suspended over your Social Security number
question.affirm: Yes. Benefits aren't suspended by text, so the claim itself gives it away.
question.gently: The case number is there to feel official. The giveaway is the claim itself.

scenarios.name: Customs fee on a package
scenarios.content: Intl Shipping Customs: shipment 7740-2219-US is held pending import duty of $12.60. Pay within 3 days or a storage fee applies: {link}

tells.note: Shops and carriers tell you about duties at checkout or on delivery, not in a surprise text.
A small, exact amount feels routine. The real aim is your card number.
Adding a penalty is another way to hurry you.

next_steps: I'll check the order on the shop's own website if I'm expecting something.
I won't pay a customs fee from a link in a text.
I'll delete it.
scenarios.learning_objective: Surprise customs fees by text are a variation on the delivery fee scam.
scenarios.debrief: This is a close cousin of the redelivery fee scam, with a shipment number to look official. Most people don't know how customs fees work, which is what makes it believable.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A surprise text asking for a customs fee through a link
question.affirm: Right. A surprise fee through a link is the sign.
question.gently: The shipment number is there to look official. The clearest sign is the surprise fee through a link.

scenarios.name: Shared photos sign-in
scenarios.content: Someone shared "Family Photos 2026" with you. Sign in with your email and password to view them: {link} Link expires in 48 hrs.

tells.quote: Sign in with your email and password
tells.note: A sign-in page reached from a text link is how passwords are collected. Your email password unlocks your other accounts.
A real share says who it's from. 'Someone' keeps it vague so you'll assume it's family.
A personal-sounding file name is bait.

next_steps: If I'm expecting photos, I'll ask the person directly whether they sent them.
I won't type my email password into a page I reached from a text.
If I already did, I'll change my password and ask someone to help.
scenarios.learning_objective: Fake shared-photo texts collect email passwords.
scenarios.debrief: Whoever has your email password can reset nearly every other password you have. Asking the person who supposedly sent it is the quickest check.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: It doesn't say who shared it and asks for your email password
question.affirm: Yes. A vague 'someone' and a request for your password is the pattern.
question.gently: The details make it feel personal. The sign is that it doesn't say who, then asks for your password.

scenarios.name: Bank fraud team and a "safe account"
scenarios.content: Fraud Prevention: following up on this morning's alert. A branch employee may be involved in fraud on your account. Reply YES and we'll call to help you move your savings to a secure account. Don't discuss with branch staff.

tells.quote: following up on this morning's alert
tells.note: Pretending to continue an earlier conversation makes you think you've already checked.

tells.quote: move your savings to a secure account
tells.note: A real bank never asks you to move money to keep it safe.
Branch staff would tell you it's a scam. That's why they don't want you talking to them.

next_steps: I'll call the number on the back of my card.
I'll never move money to a 'secure account' for anyone.
I'll tell someone in the family before I move any money.
scenarios.learning_objective: Banks never ask you to move money to a 'safe account' or keep it from branch staff.
scenarios.debrief: The 'safe account' scam is one of the most expensive, because people move savings believing they're protecting them. Any request to move money to keep it safe is the scam.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: Being asked to move savings and not tell branch staff
Being told about a fraud alert
The text arriving in the morning
question.affirm: Exactly. Moving money to keep it safe, kept from the branch, is the scam.
question.gently: Real banks do send fraud alerts, which is why this works. The giveaway is moving your savings and keeping it from the branch.

scenarios.name: Order shipped to a strange address
scenarios.content: Order #114-3920-5581 shipped: 65" Smart TV, $1,149.00, to 2290 Lakeview Dr Apt 4B. Not you? Reply NO to cancel and speak with support.

tells.note: A strange address makes you worry someone is using your account, so you reply to fix it.
This is the hook. 'Support' turns out to be the scammer.
A large purchase you didn't make is meant to alarm you into acting fast.

next_steps: I'll open the shop's app or website myself and look at my orders.
I'll check my card statement for the charge.
I won't reply to an order text I don't recognize.
scenarios.learning_objective: Fake order alerts use alarm about a stranger's purchase to reach a fake support line.
scenarios.debrief: This looks like ordinary order texts, which is why it's rated hard. The way to check is the same as always: go to the shop yourself.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: An order you didn't place, with an easy way to 'cancel' by replying
question.affirm: Yes. An order you didn't make with a convenient reply option is the setup.
question.gently: The order number looks real, which is what makes this convincing. The sign is an order you didn't place with an easy 'cancel' that reaches them.

scenarios.name: New message from your care team
scenarios.content: You have a new secure message from your care team about your recent visit, which may include test results. Sign in to the patient portal to read it: {link}

tells.note: Test results are something everyone wants to read straight away. The text never names your doctor or clinic.

tells.quote: Sign in to the patient portal
tells.note: The link leads to a look-alike sign-in page. Open the portal the way you usually do.
A real notice usually names the practice. 'Your care team' could be anyone.

next_steps: I'll open the patient portal from my own bookmark or the clinic's website.
If I'm not sure, I'll call my doctor's office.
I'll notice when a message doesn't name my doctor or clinic.
scenarios.learning_objective: Look-alike portal notices collect sign-in details; open the portal yourself.
scenarios.debrief: This is the hardest kind, because it's nearly identical to a real notice. If you always open the portal yourself, the link never matters.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: It doesn't name your doctor or clinic
question.affirm: Well spotted. Without a name, it could be from anyone.
question.gently: Real portals mention results too, so this one is genuinely hard. The small sign is that it never names your doctor or clinic.

scenarios.name: Hacker warning and a federal agent
scenarios.content: Customer Protection: your computer was accessed by an overseas group and your bank and retirement accounts may be at risk. A federal agent will call today to secure your funds. Keep this confidential, including from family.

tells.quote: A federal agent will call today to secure your funds
tells.note: Government agencies never call to help move your money.

tells.quote: Keep this confidential, including from family
tells.note: Secrecy from family is the biggest warning sign of all.

tells.quote: your computer was accessed by an overseas group
tells.note: A frightening claim you can't check is how this scam begins.

next_steps: I'll tell someone in the family straight away, whatever I've been asked.
I won't move money because of a call or text, even from someone who says they're from the government.
I'll call my bank on the number on my card.
scenarios.learning_objective: The 'phantom hacker' scam chains a tech scare, a fake bank and a fake agent to move savings.
scenarios.debrief: This is a version of what the FBI calls the phantom hacker scam. It plays out in stages, each making the next more believable. Telling family is what breaks the chain.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: Being told to keep it from family and wait for an agent to handle your money
question.affirm: Yes. Secrecy from family and an 'agent' for your money give it away.
question.gently: The scary details are there to rush you. The clearest signs are the secrecy and the agent who'll help with your money.
